t: Under the historical cost concept, land bought in 2010 for ₹2 crore and now worth ₹9 crore is normally shown in the books at:
o: ₹9 crore
₹7 crore, the appreciation only
₹5.5 crore, the average of the two
₹2 crore
e: Assets are recorded at acquisition cost and not written up for market appreciation unless a formal revaluation is adopted; this keeps the figures objective and verifiable.

t: Which of the following is a real account?
o: Capital account
Furniture account
Rent account
Commission received account
e: Real accounts relate to tangible or intangible assets; rent and commission are nominal accounts and capital is a personal account of the owner.

t: The convention of materiality permits an accountant to:
o: Ignore a ₹50 lakh claim because the insurer disputes it
Omit liabilities that are difficult to estimate
Record the proprietor's household expenses as business expenses
Charge a ₹600 calculator to expenses in the year of purchase rather than capitalise and depreciate it
e: Materiality allows insignificant items to be treated expediently; it never permits omission of significant liabilities or mixing of personal and business transactions.

topic: Accounting Process and Books of Accounts
t: The process of transferring entries from the journal or subsidiary books to the respective accounts in the ledger is called:
o: Casting
Balancing
Journalising
Posting
e: Journalising is the initial recording, posting is the transfer to ledger accounts, casting is totalling and balancing is ascertaining the net balance of an account.

topic: Accounting Process and Books of Accounts
t: Closing entries at the end of the accounting year are passed to:
o: Carry forward the balances of asset accounts to the next year
Transfer the balances of nominal accounts to the trading and profit and loss account
Record transactions that were omitted during the year
Rectify errors located after preparing the trial balance
e: Nominal accounts (expenses and incomes) are closed by transfer to the P&L account; real and personal account balances are carried forward through the balance sheet.

topic: Accounting Process and Books of Accounts
t: Goods returned by a customer who had bought them on credit are recorded in the:
o: Sales book
Sales returns book
Purchases returns book
Cash book
e: Sales returns (returns inward) are recorded in the sales returns book, from which the customer's account is credited and the sales returns account debited.

topic: Accounting Process and Books of Accounts
t: A sum of ₹9,000 paid for repairs to a vehicle was wrongly debited to the vehicle account. The rectifying entry is:
o: Debit cash account ₹9,000; credit vehicle account ₹9,000
Debit repairs account ₹9,000; credit suspense account ₹9,000
Debit repairs account ₹9,000; credit vehicle account ₹9,000
Debit vehicle account ₹9,000; credit repairs account ₹9,000
e: The vehicle account was wrongly debited, so it must be credited, and the expense that should have been debited (repairs) is now debited; the trial balance was unaffected so no suspense account is involved.

topic: Accounting Process and Books of Accounts
t: A truck costing ₹12,00,000 with an estimated life of 8 years and scrap value of ₹80,000 is depreciated under the straight-line method. The annual rate of depreciation on cost (approximately) is:
e: Annual depreciation = (12,00,000 − 80,000)/8 = ₹1,40,000, which is 1,40,000/12,00,000 = 11.67% of original cost.

topic: Accounting Process and Books of Accounts
t: The main purpose of preparing a bank reconciliation statement is to:
o: Explain the difference between the bank balance as per the cash book and as per the bank statement on a given date
Compute interest earned on the bank balance
Detect fraud committed by the bank
Replace the bank column of the cash book
e: A BRS identifies timing differences (unpresented or uncredited cheques) and errors or omissions in either record, thereby confirming the accuracy of the cash book.

topic: Accounting Process and Books of Accounts
t: A trial balance agrees even though the purchase of furniture for ₹40,000 has been debited to the purchases account. This is an example of:
o: Error of omission
Error of principle
Compensating error
Error of casting
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Treating a capital expenditure as revenue expenditure violates an accounting principle; since both debit and credit are of the same amount, the trial balance still agrees.

topic: Accounting Process and Books of Accounts
t: Which of the following statements regarding a trial balance is INCORRECT?
o: It facilitates the preparation of final accounts
It helps in detecting arithmetical errors in posting
It is a list of ledger balances prepared on a particular date
An agreed trial balance is conclusive proof that the books are free from all errors
e: Agreement of a trial balance proves only arithmetical accuracy; errors of principle, omission, commission in the wrong account and compensating errors remain undetected.

t: Under AS 9, revenue from the sale of goods is recognised when:
o: Cash is received from the customer
Significant risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred and no significant uncertainty exists about collection
The goods are manufactured and ready for despatch
The sales order is received from the customer
e: AS 9 is based on transfer of property/risks and rewards and reasonable certainty of ultimate collection, not on receipt of cash or order.

t: Under AS 22 (Accounting for Taxes on Income), a deferred tax asset arising from unabsorbed depreciation or carried-forward losses is recognised only when:
o: The company has made a profit in the current year
There is virtual certainty supported by convincing evidence that sufficient future taxable income will be available
The auditors give an unqualified opinion
The tax authorities have assessed the loss
e: AS 22 applies a stricter 'virtual certainty' test for DTA on losses, as against 'reasonable certainty' for other timing differences, because of the prudence principle.

t: AS 18 requires disclosure of:
o: Events after the balance sheet date
Transactions between the reporting enterprise and its related parties, including key management personnel
The method of valuing inventories
Segment-wise revenue and results
e: AS 18 ensures users are aware of transactions that may not have been at arm's length; segment reporting, inventories and subsequent events are covered by AS 17, AS 2 and AS 4.

t: Under AS 3, dividend paid to shareholders by a company is classified as a cash flow from:
o: Financing activities
Extraordinary items
Investing activities
Operating activities
e: Dividends paid and the issue or redemption of share capital and borrowings are financing activities since they relate to the providers of capital.

t: Under AS 26, which of the following should NOT be recognised as an intangible asset?
o: A purchased software licence with a five-year term
Internally generated goodwill
A patent acquired from another company
Copyright purchased for a specified consideration
e: Internally generated goodwill, brands and customer lists are expressly excluded because their cost cannot be reliably measured; acquired intangibles meeting the recognition criteria are capitalised.

t: Under Section 123 of the Companies Act 2013, dividend can be declared by a company out of:
o: Current year profits after providing for depreciation, or accumulated profits of previous years transferred to free reserves
Capital reserve arising on revaluation of assets
Securities premium account
Share application money pending allotment
e: Dividend must come from profits after depreciation; capital profits such as revaluation surplus and securities premium cannot be distributed.

t: Under Section 6 of the Insurance Act 1938, the minimum paid-up equity capital required to carry on general insurance business in India is:
o: ₹200 crore
₹100 crore
₹500 crore
₹50 crore
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). A life or general insurer needs ₹100 crore of paid-up equity capital, whereas a reinsurer needs ₹200 crore.

t: A capital redemption reserve must be created when a company:
o: Redeems preference shares or buys back shares out of profits otherwise available for dividend
Issues shares at a premium
Declares an interim dividend
Issues debentures at a discount
e: To preserve the capital base, an amount equal to the nominal value of shares redeemed or bought back out of free reserves is transferred to CRR, which may be used only for bonus shares.

t: Under Schedule II of the Companies Act 2013, depreciation is based on:
o: The useful life of the asset, with the residual value ordinarily not exceeding 5% of original cost
The replacement cost of the asset
A uniform 10% rate for all assets
Fixed rates prescribed by the Income-tax Act
e: Schedule II prescribes indicative useful lives and allows a residual value of up to 5% unless justified; income tax rates are separate and used only for tax computation.

t: Which of the following statements about bonus shares is correct?
o: They must be fully paid in cash by the allottees
They increase the total shareholders' funds of the company
They are issued only to preference shareholders
They capitalise accumulated profits or reserves without any cash inflow to the company
e: A bonus issue converts free reserves or securities premium into share capital; total equity remains unchanged and no cash is received.

t: Under Section 15 of the Insurance Act 1938, the audited accounts and statements must be furnished to IRDAI within:
o: Six months from the end of the period to which they relate
Three months from the end of the financial year
Twelve months from the end of the financial year
Thirty days from the end of the financial year
e: Section 15 requires the audited returns to be submitted within six months of year-end, with IRDAI empowered to extend the period in specific cases.

t: Under the IRDAI (Expenses of Management of Insurers transacting General or Health Insurance Business) Regulations 2023, the overall limit of expenses of management for a general insurer is:
o: 15% of gross written premium in India
20% of net written premium
30% of gross written premium in India
40% of gross written premium in India
e: The 2023 regulations replaced segment-wise limits with a single cap of 30% of GWP for general insurers (35% for standalone health insurers), with commission subsumed within this limit.

t: Operating expenses related to insurance business (Schedule 4) that cannot be directly identified with a segment are apportioned among revenue accounts:
o: In the ratio of claims paid
Equally among fire, marine and miscellaneous
On a reasonable and consistent basis such as net premium or gross premium, as per the insurer's disclosed policy
Entirely to the miscellaneous revenue account
e: IRDAI requires a reasonable, consistent and disclosed basis of apportionment; the common practice is in proportion to gross direct premium of each segment.

t: In the balance sheet of a general insurer (Form B-BS), 'Sources of Funds' comprise:
o: Current liabilities and provisions only
Investments, loans and fixed assets
Share capital, reserves and surplus, fair value change account and borrowings
Cash and bank balances and advances
e: The balance sheet is in vertical form: sources of funds are shareholders' funds and borrowings, while application of funds shows investments, loans, fixed assets and net current assets.

t: Under Section 12 of the Insurance Act 1938, the accounts and balance sheet of an insurer must be audited annually by:
o: The Appointed Actuary of the insurer
An officer of IRDAI
An internal auditor appointed by the Board
An auditor qualified under the Companies Act 2013
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Section 12 requires an annual audit by a qualified auditor; IRDAI additionally issues guidelines on eligibility and rotation of statutory auditors of insurers.

t: Outstanding premium due from policyholders that is more than 30 days old is relevant because:
o: It must be written off immediately in the revenue account
It is credited to premium earned only on receipt
It is shown as a contingent liability
It is generally disallowed as an admissible asset for solvency purposes
e: Under Section 64VB premium should be collected in advance; receivables beyond the permitted period (e.g. government business) are treated as inadmissible for solvency.

t: Which schedule of a general insurer's balance sheet shows 'Reserve for unexpired risk' and 'Provision for outstanding claims'?
o: Schedule 6 – Reserves and surplus
Schedule 14 – Provisions
Schedule 12 – Advances and other assets
Schedule 13 – Current liabilities
e: Technical liabilities (URR, outstanding claims, premium deficiency, taxation) are presented in Schedule 14; Schedule 6 holds shareholders' reserves and Schedule 13 current liabilities such as agents' balances and premium received in advance.

t: A general insurer's miscellaneous revenue account shows premium earned (net) ₹1,200 crore, claims incurred (net) ₹900 crore, net commission ₹60 crore, operating expenses ₹270 crore and investment income allocated to policyholders ₹150 crore. The operating result of the segment is:
o: Loss of ₹30 crore
Profit of ₹270 crore
Profit of ₹120 crore
Loss of ₹120 crore
e: Operating result = 1,200 + 150 − 900 − 60 − 270 = ₹120 crore profit; without investment income the segment would have an underwriting loss of ₹30 crore.

t: The provision for outstanding claims at the balance sheet date of a general insurer should include:
o: Only claims under litigation
Only claims that have been admitted and are awaiting payment
Claims reported but not settled, plus claims incurred but not reported (IBNR) and incurred but not enough reported (IBNER)
Claims expected on policies to be issued next year
e: Outstanding claims are provided on a case-by-case basis for reported claims, supplemented by actuarially estimated IBNR/IBNER to cover reporting and development lags.

t: Who is responsible for certifying the adequacy of IBNR reserves of a general insurer?
o: The company secretary
The statutory auditor
The Chief Financial Officer
The Appointed Actuary
e: IRDAI requires the Appointed Actuary to estimate and certify IBNR and premium deficiency reserves; the auditor relies on this certificate while auditing the financial statements.

t: A 'bordereau' in reinsurance accounting is:
o: A periodic statement listing the risks ceded or claims advised under a treaty, furnished by the cedant to the reinsurer
The reinsurer's share of the insurer's equity capital
The deposit retained by the cedant from reinsurance premium
A certificate of solvency issued by IRDAI
e: Bordereaux provide the reinsurer with details of ceded risks, premiums and claims; the premium reserve deposit is a separate concept.

t: A sliding-scale commission in a proportional treaty means that:
o: Commission is fixed at the rate charged on direct business
Commission increases each year regardless of results
Commission is paid only when the treaty makes a loss
The commission rate varies inversely with the loss ratio of the treaty between agreed minimum and maximum
e: A sliding scale rewards the cedant with higher commission when the loss ratio is low and reduces it when results deteriorate, aligning the interests of both parties.

t: A stop loss reinsurance treaty protects the cedant against:
o: Fluctuations in investment income
A single large loss on an individual risk
The insolvency of its reinsurers
The aggregate loss ratio of a class of business exceeding an agreed percentage in a year
e: Stop loss (excess of loss ratio) cover responds when total losses for the year exceed an agreed percentage of premium, unlike per-risk or per-event excess of loss.

t: An Insurance Ombudsman can entertain a complaint where the value of the claim, including expenses, does not exceed:
o: ₹20 lakh
₹30 lakh
₹50 lakh
₹1 crore
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). The limit was raised to ₹50 lakh by the amended Insurance Ombudsman Rules.

t: A general insurer's fire treaty has a premium reserve deposit of 40% retained from the reinsurer's premium and released after 12 months with interest. In the cedant's books, the amount retained is shown as:
o: Premium income of the cedant
An investment in the reinsurer's shares
A deduction from claims incurred
A liability to the reinsurer (balances due to reinsurers / deposits)
e: Premium reserve withheld belongs to the reinsurer and is released later; the cedant holds it as a liability and pays the agreed interest, which is an expense.

t: The Required Solvency Margin of a general insurer is determined as:
o: The average of RSM-1 and RSM-2
The higher of RSM-1 (premium-based) and RSM-2 (claims-based), subject to the statutory minimum
RSM-1 only, since premiums are more reliable than claims
The sum of RSM-1 and RSM-2
e: Both measures are computed segment-wise with prescribed factors; the larger aggregate becomes the RSM, with a floor of ₹50 crore (₹100 crore for reinsurers).

t: The percentage applied to incurred claims (after factors) to arrive at RSM-2 for general insurers is:
e: RSM-1 applies 20% to premiums and RSM-2 applies 30% to incurred claims (gross claims adjusted by prescribed factors or net claims, whichever is higher).

t: Minimum paid-up equity capital required for a company carrying on exclusively reinsurance business in India is:
o: ₹500 crore
₹100 crore
₹200 crore
₹50 crore
e: Section 6 of the Insurance Act prescribes ₹200 crore for reinsurers against ₹100 crore for life and general insurers.

t: If a general insurer's solvency ratio falls below the control level, IRDAI may:
o: Direct the insurer to submit a financial plan to restore the solvency position within a specified period
Take over the investments of the insurer
Require the insurer to stop paying claims
Automatically cancel the insurer's registration on the same day
e: Section 64VA empowers IRDAI to call for a financial plan and impose directions such as restrictions on new business; deregistration is a last resort, not automatic.

t: The maximum exposure of an insurer to companies belonging to a single group (other than infrastructure) is:
o: 5% of investment assets
25% of investment assets
2% of investment assets
15% of investment assets
e: Group exposure is capped at 5% of investment assets (10% for infrastructure investments), lower than the 15% industry-sector limit.

t: Investment by an insurer in the companies of its promoter group is:
o: Restricted to 5% of investment assets, with investments in unlisted promoter-group companies not permitted
Permitted only in unlisted securities
Freely permitted without any limit
Mandatory to the extent of 10%
e: To prevent conflicts of interest, promoter-group exposure is tightly capped and such investments are reported to IRDAI; loans to promoter group entities are prohibited.

t: For a debt instrument to qualify as an 'approved investment', its minimum credit rating by a SEBI-registered rating agency should generally be:
o: BBB or equivalent
A or equivalent
AA or equivalent
AAA only
e: Debt rated AA and above is approved; instruments rated between A and below AA fall under other investments subject to the 15% cap, and below A are not permitted.

t: An insurer's investment in equity shares of a listed company is shown in the balance sheet at:
o: Average of the year's highest and lowest prices
Face value plus accrued dividend
Fair value based on the last quoted closing price on the primary exchange (NSE), with BSE as secondary
Original cost in all cases
e: IRDAI prescribes NSE as the primary exchange for valuation; where a scrip is not traded on NSE, the BSE closing price is used, and unrealised changes go to the fair value change account.

t: Which of the following is a function of the Investment Committee of an insurer?
o: Approving individual insurance claims above ₹1 crore
Laying down the operational framework for investment operations and monitoring compliance with the investment policy
Appointing the statutory auditor
Fixing premium rates for new products
e: The committee frames the investment policy, approves investment limits, reviews performance and risk, and reports to the Board; claims, audit appointment and pricing lie elsewhere.

t: IRDAI's guidelines on statutory auditors of insurers require that:
o: The auditors are appointed by IRDAI directly
Only government-owned audit firms may be appointed
A general insurer has a maximum of two joint statutory auditors, each eligible for a limited tenure followed by a cooling-off period
The Appointed Actuary also acts as statutory auditor
e: IRDAI prescribes eligibility, tenure (generally five years) and rotation for joint auditors; appointment remains with the shareholders on the audit committee's recommendation.

t: The IRDAI portal through which a policyholder can escalate an unresolved grievance against an insurer is:
o: Bima Sugam
Bima Bharosa
Bima Vahak
Bima Vistaar
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Bima Bharosa (formerly IGMS) is the grievance portal; Bima Sugam is the marketplace, Bima Vahak the women-led distribution channel and Bima Vistaar the combined rural product.

t: The expense ratio of a general insurer is normally computed as:
o: Operating expenses ÷ claims paid
(Operating expenses + net commission) ÷ net written premium
Net commission ÷ investment income
Operating expenses ÷ shareholders' funds
e: The expense ratio measures the cost of acquiring and administering business relative to premium retained, and together with the loss ratio gives the combined ratio.

t: A general insurer earned profit after tax of ₹300 crore on average shareholders' funds of ₹2,500 crore. Its return on equity is:
e: Return on equity = profit after tax ÷ average net worth = 300/2,500 = 12%.

t: Which of the following ratios is a measure of an insurer's reliance on investment income to offset underwriting losses?
o: Current ratio
Debt-equity ratio
Operating ratio (combined ratio less investment income ratio)
Retention ratio
e: The operating ratio adjusts the combined ratio for investment income relative to premium; a combined ratio above 100% with an operating ratio below 100% shows investment income is subsidising underwriting.
